Just because the RISC chips had a higher clock speed did not mean that they completed any given task quicker. Since the RISC instructions were simpler and less complex they could complete less work in each instruction. A CISC chip could complete a task in one instruction that would take multiple instructions for a RISC chip.
Would the differences in instruction sets cause development to be more difficult for RISC based devices or will the compiler be able to help there?

Basically, RISC chipsets have no, (or at least fewer), convenience features built in to them. Most mainstream processors have registers for SIMD baked directly into the silicone because vector math is such a common requirement. So, basically, there are specific registers you can write vectors to and the processor will automatically do the math without the programmer needing to code those instructions himself.

It's faster, because the code being run isn't some abstract bits in cache. They are solid transistors.

So, to answer your question. Yes, programing for RISC is more difficult because of what it's name implies (REDUCED Instruction Set Computer) The instruction sets which are not included in RISC implementation need to be specifically programmed by the coder. So, for instance, the programmer can't just put an array into a register and expect it to do vector math, because there is no registers for those instructions. Therefore, the process is going to be an abstraction which is slower to process.
